cards.prompt: AI can now make a **fake voice** or a **fake video** of a real person, saying things they never said. Is each use **helpful**, or **harmful**?

items.label: Dubbing a film, with the actors' OK
Giving back a voice someone lost
A museum guide in 10 languages, with OK
A fake call that sounds like Grandma
A fake video to embarrass a classmate
A fake singer advert selling a product

cards.hint: Ask: does everyone in it know and agree, and is anyone being tricked?
cards.nudge: The same technology can help or harm. Look for whether people agreed, and whether someone is fooled.
cards.explanation: Dubbing with consent, restoring a lost voice and a museum guide **help**, and nobody's fooled. A fake Grandma call, a video to embarrass someone and a fake celebrity advert **trick or hurt** people.

cards.title: Fake faces and voices
cards.body:
A fake video or picture of a real person is a **deepfake**; a **voice clone** copies their voice. Most tools learn from many voices, then copy one from a short clip.

In Australia, sharing fake sexual images of a real person without their consent is a serious crime, and fake sexual images of anyone under 18 are always illegal.

cards.prompt: Why can a [[voice clone|voice-clone]] sometimes be made from just a short clip of someone talking?

options.text: It can only replay the exact words in the clip
options.nudge: A clone can say new words the person never said. So what does it already know?

options.text: It already learned voices from many people
It cuts words out of the clip and stitches them into new sentences
options.nudge: That would only work for words in the clip, but clones say any words at all. What does the model already know?

options.text: Short clips hold more detail about a voice than long ones
options.nudge: Longer recordings usually help, not hurt. Why might a short one still be enough?

cards.hint: Before it ever hears this person, what has the model already learned from?
cards.explanation: The model was trained on **many voices**, so it already knows how voices work. A short clip only has to show what's special about **this** voice. That's why posting your voice publicly is worth thinking about.

cards.prompt: Your friend has found an app that makes face-swap videos. Making a fake of a real person without their **permission** can hurt them, and it can spread further than you meant.

steps.text: "Let's make a video of our sports coach dancing badly and saying silly things. It's just a joke!" What do you say?

choices.text: "Only if we put 'FAKE' in tiny letters at the end"
choices.consequence: Your coach still never agreed, and a tiny label is easy to miss or crop off. It can still spread and hurt them.

choices.text: "OK, but we'll only send it to two friends"
choices.consequence: Two friends can share it with anyone. You can't control a video once it's sent.

choices.text: "No: they haven't agreed, and it could really hurt them"
choices.consequence: Right. Without permission, it isn't a joke, it's a fake of a real person.

cards.hint: Think about who has to agree before you make a fake of a real person. Does a label or a small audience change that?
cards.explanation: Without the coach's **permission**, it's a deepfake of a real person, even as a joke and even with a tiny label. And there's no such thing as "just two friends": anything sent can spread. In Australia, sharing fake sexual images of a real person without their consent is a serious crime, and fake sexual images of anyone under 18 are always illegal.

cards.prompt:
Fake videos **sometimes** have clues in the video itself, like odd blinking, but good fakes can have none. The **situation** around a video often tells you more, like whether the story makes sense. The best check: ask the real person, or a trusted source, another way.

Is each one a clue **in the video**, or **in the situation**?

items.label: Lips don't quite match the words
The voice sounds flat and odd
The edge of the face flickers
Posted by an account you don't know
No one else is reporting it

cards.hint: Could you spot it by watching closely, or by asking where it came from?
cards.nudge: Which ones could you only spot by watching the face and listening to the voice closely?
cards.explanation: Lip-sync, odd voices and flickering edges are **in the video**. Who posted it, pressure to act fast and whether anyone trustworthy is reporting it are **in the situation**, and they're often the stronger clues.

cards.prompt: A video shows a famous singer saying: "I'm giving away 1,000 free concert tickets! Click the link in the next hour."

steps.text: It looks and sounds exactly like them, and it's on a page you've never seen. What do you do?

choices.text: Click the link quickly before the tickets go
choices.consequence: The rush is the trick. The link asks for your card details. It was a deepfake advert.

choices.text: Watch closely to check the lips match the words
choices.consequence: The lips match perfectly. Good fakes pass that test. The situation (an unknown page, a rush, free tickets) is the stronger clue.

choices.text: Check the singer's official account for the same news
choices.consequence: Their official account says nothing about it, and warns about fake giveaway videos. It was a deepfake.

cards.hint: Spot the situation clues first: who posted it, and what is it pushing you to do? Then think about the best check.
cards.explanation: An unknown page, a rush and "free" are **situation clues**. The face and voice can be faked, so check the **real person's official account** or trusted news, another way.

cards.prompt: Your uncle gets a call. It sounds exactly like you, upset: "I've lost my phone and wallet. Please send money to this account, quick!" What's the **best** thing for him to do?

options.text: Hang up, then call you on the number he already has
Listen closely for a flat or robotic voice before deciding
options.nudge: A good clone can sound perfect. Is there a check that doesn't rely on this call at all?

options.text: Send a small amount first, to see if it's really you
options.nudge: Any money sent to a faker is gone, small or not. How could he check without paying anything?

options.text: Ask the caller to say his name, to prove they know him
options.nudge: Whoever chose to call him will know his name. What check goes another way, outside this call?

cards.hint: The voice can be faked. Which check doesn't go through this call?
cards.explanation: Hang up and **call back on a number he already has**. That check goes another way, so a faker can't answer it. A good clone can sound perfect, anyone calling him knows his name, and money sent to a scammer is usually gone for good.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- AI can fake a real person: **deepfakes** and **voice clones**.
- Never fake a real person without their permission.
- Situation clues beat video clues: check with the real person.

If someone fakes **you**, it's not your fault. Report it at esafety.gov.au, and tell a trusted adult. More in Stay Safe Online's free lesson **Deepfake Scams and Fakes**.
